video_title: Hedgeye Investing Summit Fall 2026 | Jim Bianco, President of Bianco Research
gist: Jim Bianco argues 5% yields are fair given roughly 5% nominal GDP, that higher rates are not bearish for stocks in a quad 2 economy, and that Fed hike risk around the October 28 meeting and new chairman Worsh's lack of forward guidance will keep volatility high. He also frames AI as a coming overbuild bubble and warns about gambling-like market structure and overpaperized gold.

themes.theme: Nominal GDP anchors the bond market

insights.claim: Bianco argues the appropriate level for interest rates is about 5% because nominal GDP growth (roughly 3% inflation plus 2% real growth) is about 5%; the 5-year note through the 30-year bond all now yield a 5 handle, so he is tentatively warming to bonds after six years of bearishness.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Bond yields near nominal growth are fair value, so the short-bonds trade has lost its easy edge and a tactical long is being considered.
insights.quote: There is a fundamental in the bond market.

insights.claim: The borrowing cost should equal the average return on a randomly chosen investment, i.e. nominal growth; rates well below that (Trump's 1-2% wish with 20% growth) subsidize below-average investments, drag on growth and cause speculative excess, inflation and malinvestment.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Too-low rates are a risk, not a free lunch; ZIRP-era assumptions should not be the baseline for valuing assets.

insights.claim: Bianco rejects one-factor explanations of yields (deficit only, inflation only, oil only); rates are the most important metric in a capitalist economy and are driven by shifting factors, including global rate and policy differentials.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Avoid two-factor models for rates; the dominant driver rotates over time.

insights.claim: Bianco says the US usually leads global yields, but currently Japan (economy rebounding off zero inflation) and France (political instability, credit risk) are pushing US yields higher rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Foreign yield pressure is a current upside driver for US long rates; watch JGB and OAT spreads.

themes.theme: Fed hike risk and the Worsh Fed

insights.claim: Odds of a Fed hike on October 28, a week before the midterms, swung from about 70% a week earlier to roughly 21-22%; Bianco thinks a hot CPI plus strong earnings and retail sales could push it back to 50% or more.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Rate-hike pricing is highly unstable around the October 28 FOMC; expect volatility into the print and election.

insights.claim: Bianco says if the market prices above 50% odds of a hike and the Fed declines, the 10-year yield could go from about 5.25% to 5.50%, because the Fed would be seen as behind the curve; the Fed needs to panic a bit more so bond traders can stop panicking.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: A dovish hold against hawkish pricing is a bear-steepening/higher-yield risk, not a relief rally.
insights.quote: bond traders can stop panicking when the Fed starts panicking

insights.claim: Since the Fed began cutting in September 2024, it cut 175bp yet the 10-year yield rose 130bp, the first time in 50-plus years a cutting cycle produced higher long-term yields; Bianco reads it as the bond market saying policy was too easy given inflation and deficits. The Fed then hiked about three weeks before this talk.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Long yields are disciplining easy policy; do not assume Fed cuts lower long rates.

insights.claim: A hot September PMI spiked the bond market's reaction because it was the first September data point, after July and August data were already strong, suggesting acceleration; GDP trackers (Atlanta Fed, New York Fed) were running hot, and Keith's nowcast has Q3 GDP above 4%.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Growth momentum is still accelerating, which supports higher yields and a hawkish bias.

insights.claim: New Fed chairman Worsh does not believe in forward guidance, so markets parse speeches from New York Fed President John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson as proxies; Williams' remarks talking down an October hike moved hike odds from about 70% to about 30%. Bianco favors ending forward guidance, noting the Fed waited until March 2022 to leave zero when inflation was 8.5%.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: With no chair guidance, Fed communication is noisier and rate vol stays elevated.

insights.claim: Inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target on every measure for about 66 months and PCE is not even below 3%; Bianco argues markets are only now questioning the transitory-supply-chain story and that this structural problem will bring more volatility.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: The 2% convergence assumption embedded in markets is the vulnerable consensus; persistent inflation keeps rate vol bid.

insights.claim: Keith's firm is long PFIX, an ETF that is a bet on bond market volatility, and says it has gone vertical; he expects more volatility if CPI pushes hike odds from 30% back toward 70%.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Rate volatility is a live, working position in Hedgeye's book.

insights.claim: Bond volatility (MOVE) and equity volatility (VIX) are constructed differently and rarely move together outside crises like COVID; Keith says macro tourists wrongly short equities on bond vol, missing that index concentration in stocks that went vertical suppresses the VIX, and Bianco adds that the yield curve shape drives MOVE.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Do not trade bond vol as an equity-short signal; VIX is suppressed by concentration.

themes.theme: Higher rates are not bearish (quad 2 vs quad 4)

insights.claim: Stocks are ignoring higher rates because rates with a 5 handle are normal relative to 5% nominal growth, not punishing; they were far too low for too long and markets are readjusting. There is little evidence the economy is buckling under them.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Rate-driven equity crash calls are weak while nominal growth supports a 5% yield.
insights.quote: very little evidence that this economy is buckling under these high interest rates right now

insights.claim: In Keith's quad 2 (growth and inflation both accelerating) bond yields and corporate profits rise together and it is bullish; he is short rate-sensitive sectors like housing and utilities. Quad 4 is where growth and profits decelerate and stocks crash.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Position on rate of change; rising yields from stronger growth are not a sell signal for stocks.

insights.claim: Keith assigns rising probability that by mid-2027 base effects bring headline inflation down sharply and growth peaks, moving to quad 4; he is still short bonds but expects to cover when the inflation and growth cycle highs are in, noting the 10-year went from 5.3% in 2007 to about 1.4% by 2012.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: The bond short has an expiry date; the turn comes when base effects roll over next year.

insights.claim: Bianco cites Rudi Dornbusch's line that expansions are murdered, not dead of old age: recessions need an event (9/11, Kuwait invasion, housing crash, pandemic), so the question each day is whether a shock just moved us from quad 2 to quad 4; recent candidates were Liberation Day, the Iran war and the Silicon Valley Bank failure, none of which did it.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Monitor for exogenous shocks rather than forecasting cyclical decay; so far recent shocks were absorbed.
insights.quote: economic expansions do not die of old age, they're murdered

insights.claim: Bianco says every technology ends its first wave in a bubble peak, and the AI marker is skepticism giving way to optimism so extreme that overbuilding becomes unavoidable, as with Global Crossings, which laid 100,000 miles of fiber with only 2% used and became the largest US bankruptcy by 2022; he argues AI is not quite there yet.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: The AI buildout is probably late-middle, not final, stage; the signal is universal optimism, not valuation.
insights.quote: Every technology that's ever been created will end its first wave in a bubble peak.

insights.claim: Technological efficiency gains complicate AI capacity forecasting: a 100 megawatt data center suddenly doing 10 times the compute would instantly create overcapacity; railroads peaked at 280,000 miles and the US now has 40% less track.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Efficiency breakthroughs, not demand slowdowns, may be the trigger for AI capex overcapacity.

insights.claim: Bianco says the US cannot decelerate AI buildout because China will not, and falling behind means a Chinese model without a white-hat period where Treasury, Fed, banks and utilities patch vulnerabilities before release; this rational logic is what produces the overcapacity.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Geopolitical arms-race framing makes AI capex persistent and overbuild likely.

insights.claim: Keith says Wall Street and Washington demand oversupply: any deceleration in capex or revenue growth gets a stock murdered, and he calls AI spending the mother of all bubbles driving index concentration and paper profits in index earnings.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Index profits and market cap are exposed to AI capex continuing; narrowing leadership adds fragility.

insights.claim: Bianco pushes back on AI extinction narratives, comparing it to airplanes or knives that are dangerous if mishandled but not species-ending.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Regulation-fear premium on AI is overdone in his view; risk is more market structure than doom.

insights.claim: Bianco says public companies have shrunk to about 4,000 from 7,000-9,000 30 years ago because firms stay private until huge (SpaceX, Anthropic at around $2 trillion), and that about 60% of options volume is zero-DTE with the CBOE introducing hourly expirations, which he calls outright gambling.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Retail-driven short-dated options and levered ETFs raise the odds of fast, mechanical unwinds.

insights.claim: Bianco notes South Korea is probably the biggest degenerate gambling market, with Samsung and SK Hynix about 50% of its stock market and widespread triple- and quadruple-levered products; he says regulators hold zero meetings on the way up and emergency ones on the way down.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: South Korea is a leveraged-concentration risk case; regulatory response is reactive.

insights.claim: Keith has gold on a bearish trend on his model because interest rates and the dollar are on bullish trends, and says gold needs rates to stop rising and speculative excess elsewhere to implode.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Gold recovery depends on a turn in rates and the dollar; no standalone bid.

insights.claim: Bianco argues gold has been overpaperized through ETFs, options, levered products and futures, citing gold up 80% and silver up 120% last year, then silver falling 40% in a day in February, and says it increasingly trades like crypto.
insights.speaker: Jim Bianco
insights.so_what: Derivative layering has made gold more volatile and flow-driven than its sound-money narrative suggests.
